Substitute the appropriately field-weighted Bianchi identity into a potential–derivative combination, complete flux squares, and inspect the surviving projected sectors. This operation supplements rather than follows from the reduced scalar potential.

Use a monotonic scalar as the evolution coordinate, expand time derivatives, impose an explicit term hierarchy, and solve the remaining algebraic trajectory equation. Here the constraint is tensor luminality and the output parametrizes single-field inflation.

Compute Schwarzschild Hawking spectra with BlackHawk, including the spin-1 graybody absorption factor rather than using a pure blackbody. The adopted temperature is T_BH=1/(8πGM_BH), and the photon spectrum peaks near 5.77 T_BH.

Factor the predicted flux into a line-of-sight halo J factor and a photon emission spectrum/rate, then integrate over the observational sky patches and energy bands. Density enters linearly for decay/PBH emission and quadratically for annihilation.

Require each candidate's emission to remain below the measured flux plus twice the reported error, which the authors use as a 95% C.L. threshold. No astrophysical diffuse component is modeled or subtracted in the main limits.

Toric divisor sections are represented by lattice-point monomials. Common coordinate factors diagnose compulsory divisor components and residual-discriminant factorization. Square-free divisors are analyzed using a section-counting formula involving complete faces and generalized genera.

Numerically minimize the anti-canonical volume subject to vol(C)≥1 for every effective curve, using Mathematica and one triangulation for each of 4319 reflexive polytopes. The resulting nonconvex quadratic optimization gives estimates of maximal gauge couplings.

Use an approximate analytic horizon-exit/observable treatment because the exact e-fold relation is not analytically solvable. Series in the implementation are truncated at n=65; the authors report that increasing this cutoff changes parameters below their code's numerical sensitivity.

Sample a seven-parameter space comprising Ω_bh², Ω_ch², 100θ_MC, optical depth τ, γ, R and V₀ with modified CosmoMC. The analysis uses flat priors, fast/slow parameter decorrelation and a Gelman–Rubin convergence diagnostic; A_s, n_s, r and N_eff are derived.

The baseline is Planck 2018 TTTEEE+lowl+lowE. Separate combinations add R19's Gaussian H₀ prior, 74.03±1.42 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, BAO, DES year-one 3×2-point data, CMB lensing or Pantheon supernova distances.
Choose heavy-field charges to cancel gauge and gravitational anomalies, extend accidental scalar phase symmetries to Yukawa interactions, and compute their QCD and electromagnetic anomalies.

Use nonlinear flavon phases and kinetic-term diagonalization to separate the eaten mode from the physical axion. Estimate explicit-breaking shifts of the axion minimum and solve one-loop hypercharge running across heavy-particle thresholds.

Differentiate the two-point function at coincident points and reduce angular integrals by isotropy. Transform diagonal Hessian entries into trace and traceless combinations, then invert the remaining two-dimensional covariance block to obtain Q.

Extract eigenvalues at a probability maximum, interpolate cumulative rank against eigenvalue, and differentiate. The authors identify the unresolved hard-edge downturn as a permanent limitation because its location recedes with N.

The source compares peak approximations with direct integrals. At N = 4, γ = 0.6, the unnormalized approximation overestimates the fixed-height integral by a nearly height-independent factor, permitting cancellation after normalization.

Integrate the scalar height analytically, leaving an eigenvalue integral weighted by a Gaussian tail. The reconstructed tail passes direct algebraic checks. The printed inconsistency concerns Eq. (4.2); no implementation or reported numerical probability is thereby independently tested.

Replace each constrained integral by a Gaussian around its own peak. The operation is applied at finite N rather than as a derived large-N expansion. Empirical small-N comparisons provide the reported accuracy evidence.

Count zeros of a vector-valued derivative using its Jacobian, then average with the local probability law. Here the vector is ∇V, its Jacobian is the Hessian, and the positive Hessian signature selects local vacua.

Expand around the explicit Λ=κ=0 solution using w=e^{-4W}, p=e^{-4φ/5}, and q=e^{-2λ}. At each curvature order solve linear inhomogeneous ODEs; the homogeneous operator is unchanged while lower-order solutions determine the sources.

Read the four-dimensional Planck coefficient from dimensional reduction of the supergravity action, and test proposed orientifold boundary-action corrections by their effects on the field equations and derivative jumps.
Estimates corona energy from the displaced Higgs potential and magnetic discharge from near-horizon monopole pair creation, approximating the emitted monopoles as point particles.

Explains massless radial fermions through descent of four-dimensional Weyl anomalies to two dimensions. Combines this mode counting with the two-dimensional thermal energy flux and the near-extremal mass–temperature relation.

Uses charged-particle Landau levels: the spin-1/2 lowest level has cancellation of the magnetic energy shift, whereas the Yang–Mills spin-1 level becomes unstable above the W-mass threshold. Flux degeneracy supplies the large number of radial modes.

Apply matching conditions equating the induced metrics and setting the extrinsic-curvature jump by brane tension. Match infrared mode coefficients across the shear-free surface, then combine the scalar spectrum with the tensor spectrum imported from the previous S-brane calculation.

Study linear scalar perturbations in longitudinal gauge, distinguishing the comoving canonical variable v from the Newtonian potential Φ and rescaled variable u. Their different growing/decaying modes during contraction make the transition prescription consequential.

Choose gauge connections as ensemble data, interpret system evolution as loop holonomy, and use the gauge action as the weight. This turns ensemble averaging into the ordinary functional integral for a single higher-dimensional theory with specified observable insertions.

Convert a compactly supported insertion into closed-boundary state preparation, compare physical states after the null quotient, and translate that comparison back to insertions. The paper applies this construction to the identity and an arbitrary globally defined bulk operator.

Insert the specific matrix-model spectral function into the local threefold equation. This operation yields a candidate topological-string geometry; the physical duality and its range of validity are imported rather than proved by the substitution.

Prepare candidate states, evaluate all Euclidean inner products including topology changes, quotient the zero-norm subspace, and complete. The paper uses this imported construction as a possible mechanism for reducing baby-universe degrees of freedom, without calculating its rank in higher dimensions.

Apply an energy cutoff to an otherwise infinite-dimensional tensor identity, using the vanishing Hamiltonian on the extra factor to preserve it under truncation. A single suitable cutoff suffices; this is not an asymptotic extrapolation.

A proposed bridge to low-energy EFT computes Γ at a scale M where perturbation theory becomes applicable, then uses perturbative evolution and matched RG schemes. Wetterich and Polchinski formulations could provide consistency checks.

The review describes the Wetterich functional flow, background-field quantization, fluctuation-vertex expansions and covariant derivative expansions. Momentum-dependent vertices and form factors provide routes toward observables.

Applies existing consistent uplift formulae to obtain warped metrics and higher-dimensional fluxes. At fixed points, integrates the six-form or seven-form flux to construct the D4 or M5 Wess–Zumino potential using constant scalars and A = r/l.

Expands the DBI plus Wess–Zumino actions for slow probes in static gauge. The resulting potentials are VD4 = e^(5A)[Δ + (√2 g l/15)U] and VM5 = e^(6A)[Δ + (l/6)U]. Their internal-coordinate dependence is used for the force test.

For supersymmetric flows, uses first-order supersymmetry equations to obtain flux-potential integrability. The appendix constructs C(5) = −e^(5A)Δ vol1,4 and C(6) = −e^(6A)Δ vol1,5, producing exact cancellation in the displayed probe potentials.
Reduce scalar quotient volume to group covolume where justified, then use nonzero adjoint trace to obstruct a lattice. Keep any symmetric-branch lattice construction separate.

Assume finite fundamental group, combine rational-point density with Wilson’s existence theorem, and contradict absence of rational curves. Infinite fundamental group then reduces the classification to A-type after excluding K-type.
Translates integral symplectic monodromy into functional equations for globally continued prepotentials; uses nilpotent-orbit and sl2-orbit theorems to discuss degeneration limits.

Lift the quotient map, decompose its Maurer–Cartan form, and translate geometric pluriharmonicity into covariant differential equations. The operation constructs tt* data rather than merely assigning a geometric name to an existing solution.

Restrict the possible cubic factors using the VHS theorem, obtain rational representatives of the real orbit types, and apply rational-group density. Projectivizing the resulting affine density gives the statement for W.

Separate three tasks: classify real orbit closures, prove that representatives can be chosen over Q, and establish density of G(Q). The application uses arithmetic light cones and Hermitian determinant-zero varieties, rather than inferring rationality from real geometry alone.
Construct the generating function in transverse charts, transform the full period vector, and track branches. A single prepotential branch cannot replace the global scalar geometry.
Lift and decompose the pluriharmonic map to obtain tt* data. Treat its explicit grading-generated twistor extension as unresolved until the exponent/Lax convention conflict is reconciled.

Interpret tt* flat sections as brane amplitudes and impose their inherited Grothendieck-group lattice. Extend the known semisimple arithmetic analysis to the local-graded sector as a proposed necessary test.

Integrate the spectral linear system, impose its real structure at ζ=1, invert the resulting matrix, and quotient by the maximal compact subgroup. Descending to X additionally requires the stated deck-equivariance relation.
Test unimodularity through a three-grade dimension count, then invoke the imported saturation characterization. The calculation does not construct a lattice.

Lift the quotient-target sigma model to E×K and apply its (4,4) nonrenormalization theorem. This operation concerns protected prepotential corrections, rather than a claim that every quantum observable on the quotient is uncorrected.
Verify completeness, sectional-curvature sign and lattice irreducibility, then apply Eberlein rigidity to the full isometry group.

Reformulates special geometry through local-graded tt* systems and pluri-harmonic maps. Physical half-BPS brane categories supply integral structures through their numerical and K-theoretic invariants.

Integrate a genus-one anomaly, constrain the holomorphic ambiguity by modularity and boundary behavior, and evaluate its cusp slope. Each stage needs separate input; interior holomorphy and modularity alone do not state the necessary cusp-growth condition.
Uses Griffiths period maps, semisimplicity of the monodromy group's Q-Zariski closure, and VHS rigidity. The dichotomy argument studies monodromy-invariant real Lie subalgebras.

Imposes integer flux periods and Romans-mass quantization, using Gauss–Bonnet to connect curved two-manifold volumes with curvature. This distinguishes supergravity solutions from those satisfying the additional quantum flux conditions.

Constructs the intersecting-brane solution by harmonic superposition, takes its near-horizon limit and integrates RR fluxes to relate harmonic-function coefficients to integer brane charges. Smearing on T6 means the intermediate coefficients Nα are not simply the brane numbers nα.

Reduces the ten-dimensional Einstein, dilaton and form equations to algebraic constraints on invariant flux coefficients. Eliminating the dilaton constraint gives curvature inequalities; in the five-factor ansatz the relevant combinations are expressed as sums of squares.

The entropic criterion is applied to metric f(R) field equations and illustrative Hu–Sawicki and Nojiri–Odintsov models. For interacting dark energy, an assumed Hubble-history ansatz is used to translate entropy and quantum-stability requirements into restrictions on Q.

The central argument inserts transitions between an empty vacuum and an N-hairon state into vacuum bubbles and propagators. It assigns overlap exp(−N), yielding an asserted exp(−2N) correlator suppression, and subsequently interprets loop corrections through thermal field theory.
FLRW continuity and evolution equations are rewritten as an autonomous system. Fixed points are perturbed using dV/dN = KV; the dark-energy-dominated point is assigned eigenvalues 3w and 3(w+1).

The author eliminates horizon data using the extremality relation, obtains the classical dimension Δ(q), and compares Δ(2q) with Δ(q). Small- and large-charge expansions and fixed-Δ expansions at large or small c characterize the resulting curve.

The four-point function of charges q,q,−q,−q is decomposed by the operator product expansion into conformal blocks. Crossing equations and positivity of squared OPE coefficients are formulated as a numerical semidefinite program, bounding the lowest-energy operator in the T+ sector.

Vacuum bubbles and Higgs propagators are replaced by thermal-state correlators. Thermal field-theory power counting is combined with overlaps between empty and hairon-filled vacua, assigned exp(−S) approximately exp(−N), to argue for suppression of UV contributions.

A wave-function expansion in hairon-number or cosmological-constant states is followed by a subsystem/environment density-matrix construction. The author traces over hidden states and compares coherent transition probabilities with a proposed diagonal density matrix lacking interference terms.
Solve geodesics on symmetric scalar cosets through the exponential map and classify extremal trajectories by the nilpotency degree of their Noether charge matrix.
Discuss fragmentation through D-instanton probe actions and a reported quadratic fluctuation analysis using gauge-invariant variables with fixed axion momentum at the boundary.
Reduce radial scalar equations to affinely parametrized geodesics using a harmonic function h. Their constant squared velocity c is the only scalar datum entering the universal Einstein constraint.

Construct and solve the background-dependent fluctuation equation before inferring scale separation. Compare physical eigenvalues with moduli masses rather than identifying every KK mass with one inverse radius.

Differentiate masses at fixed level and specified independent background data, integrate out the retained tower, and match the estimated loop metric to the tree metric. Local conifold derivatives hold volume, flux/coupling data, and throat boundary data fixed; derivatives along a vacuum family are different operations.
Stabilize flux-sensitive fields, add Ae^−aT to fix the Kähler modulus in AdS, then reanalyze the coupled system after introducing a warped antibrane uplift.

Introduce an auxiliary variable, add weak dynamics, and evaluate geometric constraints near its proposed low-energy solution. Conclusions concern this particular extension and require checking its approximation to the original effective theory.
Calculate speed, normalize velocity, differentiate the tangent covariantly, and contract with the metric. Here the approximate trajectory is (φ,X), and the metric is diag(P_X,Λ⁻⁶).

Minimize the positive Λ⁶ contribution to the squared potential gradient by choosing the smallest proposed matching scale. The source implements this through near saturation of its leading auxiliary correction estimate.

Solve the corrected mass formula for ε and differentiate with respect to entropy, pressure, charge or an individual ci while fixing the stated other variables. Multiply inverse derivatives by their conjugate potentials and compare with the extremal mass derivative.

Express M in terms of horizon radius, charge, couplings and ε. Apply the chain rule along an extremal branch; the horizon-radius contribution is multiplied by T and vanishes at T=0. The paper also describes direct differentiation after solving T=0 for r+(ε).

Normalize fields, isolate a common-exponent charge sector, evaluate the dilatonic bound, and project the resulting logarithmic mass gradient onto the selected geodesic. Keep the charge frame and fixed discrete labels explicit.

Choose an ordered degeneration, decompose fixed charges, read norm and mass powers, normalize the leading metric, and sum normalized quadratic contributions by phase. Hold spectator moduli fixed throughout the limit.

Group adapted period terms by real or imaginary phase, sum normalized quadratic contributions, and extract radii. Preserve the selected charge sector when converting these radii into further inequalities.

Replace exact periods by their nilpotent orbit, retain the dominant monomial in an ordered boundary sector and differentiate it to obtain leading field metrics. Track spectator coordinates and discarded exponential corrections.

Integrate the specified linear charged tower to a self-consistent species cutoff and compare induced kinetic terms. The approximate cutoff prevents establishing the numerical equality required for exact force matching.
Construct the potential, follow the radial BPS branch and test its endpoint. Distinguish charge admissibility from microscopic population and stability under motion through moduli space.

Identify the sector and physical saturating tower, match the force and extremality relations, derive canonical mass gradients, and project along the actual trajectory. Establish any numerical lower bound through a separate spectrum and projection argument.

Whiten the charge metric before constructing the mass quadric. This preserves the physical vector norm and makes the extra conditions behind exactly two finite radii and the simple eigenvalue formulas explicit.
Construct a candidate W and verify its reality, full potential identity, and scalar flows. Commutation with the Hodge matrix is a source-proposed shortcut requiring additional conditions.

Perturb H(phi), retain first order at fixed V, and inspect the accumulated exponent along the rolling direction. This is a local homogeneous stability operation whose kinetic normalization must agree with the background equations.
The paper applies this standard mode operation to z=a dot phi/H on a high-energy brane background. It retains acceleration-parameter powers, while treating epsilon and the Bessel index approximately.

Input the expansion law, canonical kinetic energy, and acceleration constraint; eliminate cosmic time using phi, solve for H(phi), and reconstruct the potential. Consistent coefficients are essential when translating among these outputs.
Evaluate the model at horizon crossing, compare its r–n_s point with published contours, retain admissible beta–N pairs, and normalize the remaining integration constant using the scalar amplitude.

Expand the mass function, construct scalar and gravitational exchange between massive states, and compare common-distance coefficients. This differs from integrating out massive exchange into the local quartic of the single-field calculation.

Compare scalar and gravitational conversion at threshold using the asserted massless enhancement. The packet does not provide the tensor-amplitude calculation needed to establish its numerical coefficient.

Expand the potential, sum its contact diagram and all three cubic-exchange diagrams, and match the near-threshold amplitude to a number-conserving quartic. Positive mass and the absence of omitted leading interactions are essential.

A Jacobi matrix A obeys a curvature-dependent second-order equation with A(p)=0 and A′(p)=identity; det A=0 detects conjugacy. The authors use G=√det A and the expansion θ to connect this construction to Raychaudhuri focusing.

For the generalized argument, the authors construct RΛ=∫θΛ²dλ and uΛ=1/RΛ, asserting u′Λ=−(uΛIΛ−1)²≤0. Monotonicity and zeros of u are used to argue persistence and continuity of nearby conjugate points.

An auxiliary complete Riemannian metric supplies compact distance balls. A radius function f enclosing an initial point and a conjugate pair is asserted to be upper semicontinuous; its maximum over null initial data above compact K produces K′.

Use field redefinitions to remove redundant four-derivative operators and dualize the axion into a two-form gauge field. The Euclidean two-form action has scalar and flux terms (∂φ)²/2+exp(−βφ)H²/(12f²), simplifying the charged saddle calculation.

Evaluate the leading correction as ΔSn=ΔSE[Φ(0)]+O(Δ²). The first variation of the two-derivative action gives no leading contribution because the background satisfies its equations and the relevant boundary term vanishes.

Apply forward-scattering positivity to s–u symmetric amplitudes formed from arbitrary real axion–dilaton superpositions. The appendix reduces the resulting family of inequalities to an allowed region for a1,…,a4.
The geometric analysis uses Hodge index and Lefschetz theorems, Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch, and minimal-surface inequalities to relate divisor invariants to central charges and gauge-rank bounds.

Count M5 zero modes on a smooth ample surface with b₁=0, separating tensor chirality and fermionic contributions. Add translations and compare the resulting central charges with the inflow formula through the intersection dictionary.

Move away from a non-Abelian enhancement locus, assign masses using root and weight pairings with Cartan scalars, and integrate out the massive fermions. The outputs are Abelian effective couplings usable in string anomaly calculations.

Bulk anomaly inflow from cubic and mixed gravitational Chern–Simons terms determines worldsheet anomalies. The calculation smooths the magnetic source using global angular forms and applies descent relations to gauge and Lorentz variations.

Regularize a codimension-three magnetic source, vary the topological bulk action, and integrate angular-form identities over the linking sphere. The operation determines anomaly coefficients without requiring a microscopic worldsheet Lagrangian.

Compute the minimum left-moving central-charge cost of the currents required on a string and compare it with the available interacting central charge. A shortfall obstructs the required unitary anomaly-canceling worldsheet, conditional on BPS completeness.

Identify the infrared superconformal symmetry before converting anomalies to central charges. Remove the ordinary free center-of-mass multiplet, then compare the interacting central charge with the cost of the currents that actually reside in that sector.

Uses modified SimpleMC MCMC calculations of expansion rates and distances with compressed Planck, BAO, supernova and cosmic-chronometer data. Sampling priors are flat over Ωm0∈[0.05,0.5], Ωb0h0²∈[0.02,0.025] and h0∈[0.4,1.0].

Decomposes the stress tensor into density, isotropic pressure and trace-free anisotropic pressure; projects conservation equations and compares Einstein density, average-pressure and shear-propagation equations with the Friedmann–Klein–Gordon system. Redshift parametrization then reconstructs the effective components.

Reduce in Einstein frame and track kinetic terms through field-dependent rescalings before comparing forces. Gauge and Yukawa matching check algebraically; the full scalar–radion force requires resolving terms omitted from the later diagonal action.

Cancel the fermion anomaly through axionic variations, determine vector masses, and retain massless exchange. An anomaly-free generator becomes relevant to a long-range weak-gravity test only after its masslessness is established.
Solve the anomaly equations, preserve charge normalization, and restrict the kinetic matrix. Separately determine whether the selected directions remain massless before evaluating their force.

Compares a direct 5D wave-function/boundary-condition calculation with a 4D construction using free KK profiles and an infinite fermion mass matrix. Bi-diagonalization determines physical masses; the Yukawa matrix must be rotated separately.

Uses distribution theory and weak derivatives to obtain brane junction terms and conditions for discontinuous fields. Adapts this framework to star/rose graphs and performs Klein–Gordon and massless Dirac KK decompositions.

Applies Hamilton’s principle with boundary variations, Noether currents, and essential or natural boundary conditions. Bilinear boundary terms (BBTs) modify the variational problem to avoid imposing incompatible conditions on both fermionic chiralities.

Compare corrected and uncorrected near-extremal mass and entropy numerically, varying electric charge, deformation ε and AdS radius l. These comparisons supply the paper's evidence for the direction of entropy and mass shifts.

Express mass and temperature using horizon entropy, solve the mass formula for ε, and differentiate with specified quantities fixed. At extremality, use T=0 and a chain rule for Mext(S(ε),ε), avoiding an explicit solution for extremal entropy that the authors describe as difficult.

Numerically evolve the full background equations to compare εV, Q and energy densities. In particular, compare quadratic and quartic potentials with an inverse-temperature coefficient against a quartic example using the full microscopic VWLI coefficient.

Use the slow-roll background equations 3H(1+Q)φ̇≈−V′, ρR≈3Qφ̇²/4 and 3H²≈V/MPl². Derive the evolution of Q and d ln εV/dN=(4εV−2ηV)/(1+Q), then combine these rates to obtain parameter inequalities for exit.

The paper propagates equality-saturating ζ histories from an allowed present-day interval and tests the NEC strip and the integrated BBN constraint. No trajectory computation is independently executed in this extraction.

Propagate equality trajectories from allowed endpoints, test strip crossing, and evaluate a cumulative observable. Here the variable is ζ, the driver is w(a), and the cumulative observable is the BBN-to-present Newton-constant ratio.

Average internal equations with a positive e^{AΩ} measure, redefine the effective scale factor, and express external expansion through ρ₄d and p₄d. Application requires the source's imported gauge and dimensional-reduction assumptions.

Massless-dipole stellar bounds are translated from axion emission using the nonrelativistic spin-dependent amplitudes and a factor of two for vector polarizations. For particles mixing with ordinary photons, the review instead requires thermal polarization tensors and plasma effects.

Diagonalization of Abelian kinetic and mass terms distinguishes available field rotations. Effective dipole operators describe massless-photon interactions; integrating out scalar messengers and dark fermions matches a simplified UV model onto these operators.

Relic abundance is related to thermally averaged annihilation through the Boltzmann equation and freeze-out approximations. Experimental coverage combines resonance searches, displaced vertices, missing energy/momentum/mass, and dark-matter scattering searches.
Establish Kähler geometry through an integrable complex structure and a closed Hermitian form. Compute Ricci curvature using a tridiagonal determinant recursion and −∂∂̄log det g.

Rewrite the η-deformation using auxiliary fields and homogeneous coordinates, then T-dualize all angular directions to eliminate the B-field. Legendre transformation of toric Kähler potentials provides the undeformed benchmark.

Apply a generalized Pohlmeyer map, require its coupled equations to admit a common Lagrangian, and mechanically reduce them. For the selected exponential potential, a linear field rotation separates two independent systems, supplying the second mechanical integral.

Simplify the exterior metric using small quantum parameters, introduce a solution-dependent rescaled time τ, and examine metric and curvature falloff. Evaluate separate energy surface integrals using the spatial metric and spatial Ricci tensor, with lapse adapted to the exact Killing field.

Introduce Eddington–Finkelstein-type coordinates and compare metric coefficients and their first two derivatives from the interior and exterior. The finite positive horizon limit of the relevant coefficient product permits a regular coordinate description across the horizon.

Wick rotate the static exterior and fix the Euclidean-time period by removing the conical singularity. Thermal Green-function periodicity then supplies the temperature for a test quantum field; this method does not require field equations for the background metric.

Use Cauchy’s formula, analyticity, Hermitian analyticity and the generalized optical theorem to express the IR-subtracted amplitude tensor as a positively weighted integral of intermediate-state amplitude products plus crossed terms.

Apply Wigner–Eckart decomposition to separate dynamics from Clebsch–Gordan coefficients. Symmetrized irrep projectors generate potential extremal rays; taking their conical hull identifies the actual extremal rays.

Invoke extremal representations of salient cones and finite-generator polyhedral geometry. Dual-cone witnesses establish inequalities; convex-hull exclusion and linear optimization infer necessary UV contributions. Reverse-search algorithms and linear programming are suggested for larger problems.

Fourier modes are treated through an asymptotic WKB expansion organized by adiabatic order. The off-shell leading frequency uses arbitrary mass M; m and M count as order zero, while Δ²=m²−M² is assigned order two.

Define the renormalized EMT by subtracting its order-0-through-4 expansion at M from its on-shell expression at m. A second route uses dimensional regularization and gravitational counterterms, followed by the same adiabatic subtraction; minimal subtraction alone is not the final prescription.

Uses high-temperature loop expansions of the effective potential. Modulus-dependent gauge couplings generate a leading T^4 inverse-modulus contribution; the adopted thermal model also contains a negative, modulus-independent T^4 term, with positive coefficients.

Estimates displacements by linearizing the potential gradient around its minimum. Tracks component densities through epochs with specified equations of state, and matches horizon exit to later expansion using entropy conservation. Compares three approximate destabilization criteria: barrier energy, vanishing mass, and displacement to the barrier.

Performs partial numerical Floquet analysis of linear fluctuations about periodic homogeneous modulus oscillations. Expansion and decay are neglected, making the background periodic and temperature constant; multipliers are obtained from two independent fluctuation solutions.

Reconstruction equates both the energy density and equation of state of THDE to those of a canonical scalar: ρφ=V+φ̇²/2 and pφ=−V+φ̇²/2. The resulting equations are solved for φ(t) and V(φ), followed by plots against redshift and field value.

The paper specializes the gravitational field equations to flat FRW, reduces them to an equation for H, and reports power-law expansion. It then combines the THDE density with the continuity equation and pΛ=ωΛρΛ to obtain an equation of state.
Uses a dimensional rate estimate Γ∼H³/M_P² to motivate an inverse-rate timescale. Compares this with an imported logarithmic entanglement timescale and the proposed logarithmic censorship bound.

For a hard excitation with energy comparable to a Hubble patch, compares three parametric suppression estimates: Gibbons–Hawking Boltzmann weighting, entropy loss, and a coherent-state many-soft-to-few-hard graviton transition using an imported amplitude.

Models field modes as oscillators with expansion-driven frequency changes at rate H. A proton-decay photon produced alongside a de Sitter graviton illustrates why backward extrapolation of a real particle past its production event can be misleading.

Use G₂-form identities and representation projectors, enforce unit volume with a superfield Lagrange multiplier, and solve critical-point equations for P or V. Numerical critical points and noncanonically normalized Hessians diagnose stabilization in the retained scalar sector.

Dimensionally reduce the 10D action, apply RR tadpole conditions, and match kinetic terms and the scalar potential to a real-superpotential formulation. The superpotential is guessed and checked against the reduced potential rather than derived from the full 10D supersymmetry transformations.

Components declare required and provided quantities. Interfaces and introspection determine dependencies and execution order; caching permits reuse when a parameter change leaves a component's direct and indirect inputs unchanged.

Includes adaptive Metropolis–Hastings MCMC, fast-block oversampling and dragging, a PolyChord nested-sampling interface, minimizers, and importance reweighting. MCMC convergence uses a modified Gelman–Rubin R−1, with optional stopping checks on confidence-limit dispersion.

Parameters sharing recalculation footprints form blocks. A lower-triangular Cholesky transformation allows slow updates to mix with faster parameters while preserving fast-only updates. For ordering σ, cumulative footprints D(F)=min(1,LᵀF) give cycle cost T(σ)=n_σ·D(F_σ)t, minimized over permutations.

The gravitational framework uses the Noether identity for volume-preserving diffeomorphisms, a local application of the Poincaré lemma, and Bianchi identities. Specified diffusion–density relations then close the cosmological equations for analytical integration.

Background fits use 51 observational Hubble measurements over 0.07≤z≤2.36, including 31 differential-age measurements and remaining BAO measurements treated as independent, together with 1048 Pantheon supernovae. Affine-invariant MCMC uses 24 chains, 4500 steps, and 1500 preceding burn-in steps.

Gaussian likelihoods combine datasets through additive χ². The supernova analysis includes statistical and systematic covariance and eliminates the magnitude nuisance parameter by minimization, yielding A−B²/C. AIC and BIC compare fits while penalizing additional parameters.

Quasinormal modes are obtained through Chebyshev pseudospectral discretization and a generalized eigenvalue problem, using 50 gridpoints and 60-digit precision; convergence is reported by the authors. Diffusivities are extracted from low-momentum imaginary dispersion or hydrodynamic formulas with Kubo-derived coefficients.

An analytical neutral N=3 calculation solves the zero-frequency shear equation near the zero-temperature limit, imposes horizon regularity, and extracts the shear modulus from the boundary expansion. This supplies a limiting analytical check on crystal diffusion.

The upper-bound argument compares diffusive spread √(Dt) with a causal distance vlightcone t at equilibration. An Israel–Stewart telegraph-equation illustration gives D≤c²τπ when its asymptotic propagation is subluminal.

At first order in α, decompose the metric perturbation into trace and transverse-traceless parts. The latter obeys the homogeneous Lichnerowicz equation; the remaining volume/dilaton perturbation satisfies ∇²ϕ^(1)=(α̂/16)R_GB². Other background moduli decouple at this order.

Use semi-flat, hyperkähler and Taub–NUT descriptions near the cores, perturbative matching of induced metrics and extrinsic curvatures, and numerical integration in the outer region. Outer evolution is fully nonlinear despite perturbative matching data.

Construct the periodic-T3 spin nulbordism from a rational elliptic surface with a tubular neighborhood of a generic torus fiber removed. Its Weierstrass discriminant has degree 12; fiber degenerations become local KK-monopole cores.

Reviews attempts to destroy horizons through charged or spinning test bodies, test fields and matter shells. Effective potentials, self-force or backreaction, and formation of a larger shielding horizon can change conclusions drawn from simpler approximations.

Uses coupled Hawking mass loss and Schwinger discharge models to discuss trajectories in charge-to-mass ratio. For dilatonic GHS black holes, the review discusses a modified charge-loss ansatz and a near-extremal expansion, rather than a general evaporation theorem.

Distinguishes curvature diagnostics, including Ricci and Kretschmann scalars, from causal geodesic incompleteness at finite proper time or affine parameter. The latter is the singularity notion used in the stated Penrose theorem.

For domain walls, solves second-order equations for four scalars and the warp function A(r), together with a Hamiltonian constraint. Numerical integrations begin with regular IR expansions and scan integration constants after using radial-shift freedom.

Scans the scalar potential for critical points, computes scalar masses in the seven-chiral sector to identify BF violations, and uses full N = 8 mass formulae for the remaining previously known candidates.

Pulls back the Einstein-frame DBI and Wess–Zumino actions to probe-brane worldvolumes and extracts radial potential densities. Higher-brane calculations include B-field-induced lower RR charges and obtain C5, C7 and C9 recursively from democratic RR duality relations.

A qualitative fluid-jet analogy motivates continuation after neck breakup: molecular dynamics resolves a tiny hydrodynamic failure, followed by resumed fluid evolution; quantum gravity is proposed to play the analogous local role before Einstein evolution resumes.

The essay classifies violations by the mass concentrated in the high-curvature region relative to the initial mass. It suggests surrounding that region on a spatial slice and assigning a suitable quasilocal mass, such as Brown–York energy or Hawking mass.

Its timescale reasoning contrasts tclass∼GM/c³ with tevap∼tPlanck(M/MPlanck)³. Whether formation time stays finite or diverges as the Planck cutoff is removed distinguishes the fast classical violations under discussion from slow quantum evaporation.

Numerically diagonalizes representation-projected scalar mass matrices in Mathematica through level n = 6. The authors report checks against massless Goldstone modes and reproduction of lower even levels when using traceful harmonics at n = 6; these are reported checks, not independently reproduced here.

Rewrites the scalar mass matrix in SU(8)-covariant form using fermion shifts A1 and A2. Harmonics are symmetric traceless SO(8) representations [n,0,0,0]; tensor products with the truncation fields are branched under SO(3) × SO(3), with eaten scalar/vector representations removed.

Uses previously developed Exceptional Field Theory spectroscopy: expand linear fluctuations as truncation modes times scalar harmonics of the maximally symmetric compactification, then dress the embedding tensor and harmonic generators with the vacuum scalar matrix. Higher-dimensional input is required only at the maximally symmetric point.

Cross imported Compton relations to pair production, retain the external species and charge sector, and apply the kinematic prefactor. Evaluate threshold with background and couplings fixed. The cited derivation and complete crossing dictionary are not reproduced.

Compare complete pure nongravitational and gravitational tree amplitudes for the same final particles. Approach threshold at fixed background, species, charge or brane sector, and couplings; include exchange and contact terms before translating the proposed comparison into a bound.

Integrate out a specified tower up to the species cutoff, estimate its kinetic correction, and impose order-one infrared emergence. The paper applies this procedure to fermions while retaining the imported emergence assumption.

Assign topology weights, convert Ms/Mp to a gs power, canonically normalize the external fields, and read the normalized Yukawa exponent. The paper uses this standard operation rather than developing a new normalization method.

Integrate the bulk action over a circle, match the gravitational coefficient, normalize the light fields, and compare the interaction-derived scale with compactification-induced supersymmetry breaking.

Blow up base points, potentially in several stages, to resolve the configuration of singular-fiber components. These operations also describe sections; the paper imports the statement that sections arising from base-point blow-ups generate the building block's Mordell–Weil group.

Apply Mukai's projective-duality construction to the pair consisting of a cubic hypersurface X₃ in P⁸ and the Segre variety Y₆ = P² × P² in P⁸. Four hyperplanes restricted to Y₆ correspond on the dual side to four points spanning P³, producing a cubic surface.

A 3 × 3 determinantal representation of the cubic supplies the four (1,1) equations: each matrix position represents a bilinear coordinate monomial, and the coefficient of each cubic coordinate determines the corresponding Hᵢ. The matrix need not be symmetric.

Solve the warp-factor Poisson equation on the torus using a generalized Green function with its constant mode removed. A Jacobi-theta integral regularizes the nonconvergent naive Fourier series; near-source asymptotics fix the additive constant, and field profiles support the approximation analysis.

Reduce the ten-dimensional bulk flux terms and O6 DBI contribution to a seven-dimensional dilaton–volume action. Using the tadpole and negative O6 tension gives a total-square no-scale potential with one flat scalar combination.

Use a perturbative expansion in κ, pointwise comparisons of action densities along the same trial path, and subsequent minimization. A separate on-shell derivative with respect to κ establishes action monotonicity; boundary and moving-endpoint terms must be handled.

Minimize S[Vt]=(6π²/κ²)∫(D+Vt′)²/(Vt²D)dφ, where D²=Vt′²+6κ(V−Vt)Vt. Stationarity supplies the tunneling-potential equation of motion. The underlying functional is imported from the author's earlier formulation.

Solve the first-order D=0 equation for critical curves. Algebraically it gives Vc=Vt−Vt′²/(6κVt), reproducing earlier critical-potential forms. Domain-wall profiles follow by quadratures from φ̇=√[2(V−Vt)] and ρ̇/ρ=−√(−κVt/3); multifield paths additionally obey a covariant transverse equation.

Use the dimer dictionary: faces encode gauge factors, edges encode bifundamental or adjoint chiral fields, and nodes encode superpotential terms. Orientifolds act as Z₂ involutions of the graph, with fixed-line signs determining projections of gauge groups and matter.

Choose anomaly-free ranks, take the fractional-brane IR limit, and identify the resulting strong dynamics with known gauge theories. Seiberg duality relates toric phases. The retained cubic interaction is H_int=(M_Pl²/2)∫d³x ε_H²aζ²∂²ζ. Selection neglects nonlocal terms, terms containing ζ̇ after super-Hubble freeze-out, and higher slow-roll orders.

Leading perturbative entropy uses −λ²ln(λ²) times squared interaction matrix elements divided by squared excitation-energy gaps, with λ=√ε_H/(2√2aM_Pl). Appendix B supplies an approximate time-dependent treatment for the dominant configuration.

Two-mode squeezing describes quadratic evolution. Tracing out sub-Hubble modes and separately suppressing number-basis off-diagonal entries provides the coarse-grained density matrix used for the squeezing-entropy calculation.

Start from the divergent internal measure, impose a finite radial endpoint or an integrable warp weight, and recompute the effective gravitational coupling. In this paper both are proposed prescriptions; the warp profile and global completion are not constructed.

Propagate a joint confidence contour through a specified family of observable histories, then maximize pointwise. Here the operation maps a two-parameter dark-energy contour to an upper function of redshift; its application to other histories requires a separate statistical justification.

Normal ordering in time-dependent adiabatic ladder operators subtracts the vacuum two-point function: the renormalized bilinear contains |φ|²−|φad|². The paper uses leading-order adiabatic modes; subtraction is necessary for the electric response to vanish as m→∞.

Evaluate the leading in-in contribution using the cubic interaction Hamiltonian. Exact charged-scalar modes are parabolic cylinder functions, selected by positive-frequency WKB behavior in the remote past. At this order the approach parallels a Bogolyubov-coefficient calculation.

Regulate the KK sums with independent cutoffs N±. Mellin–Barnes representations and Hurwitz-zeta-like sums isolate divergent constants and reconstruct convergent parabolic-cylinder series. The adiabatic contribution is rewritten using Jacobi theta functions and modified Bessel K1 functions.
Expand potential and canonical slope in specified superpotential and Kähler hierarchies, then impose both energy positivity and the radial acceleration criterion.
Compute the thermal functions before expanding in mass over temperature. Preserve their field-dependent validity: light states stabilize the origin, while heavy states decouple near a distant vacuum.
Compute a metric and F-term potential from K and W, specify a real trajectory, and test energy sign, canonical slope, and transverse curvature within the same retained approximation.

String classification counts unit-winding φ₂ strings within separation s=4η₁⁻¹ along φ₁ strings. Statistics use segment lengths; the reported reference fractions average ten realizations, with standard deviations as error bars.

Collision initial data combine numerically obtained static axial strings after rotation and Lorentz boosts, in Lorenz gauge. Typical velocity is 0.7 and relative angle 0.2π; a small-angle example uses 0.06π. Runs stop before collision disturbances reach imposed boundaries.

Network evolution uses temporal gauge, periodic spatial boundaries, leap-frog time integration, and second-order spatial finite differences. Initial scalar fluctuations follow a Planck distribution at T=√3η₁; gauge-field derivatives satisfy the constraint equation.

Compute finitely many relative BPS coefficients by mirror symmetry and fit modular ansätze to obtain proposed all-order expressions. Extract anomalies from the q0 coefficient of the appropriate fugacity expansion and compare modular one-loop Green-Schwarz integrals with geometric couplings.

Define genus-zero fourfold Gromov-Witten invariants using a four-form insertion integrated over the virtual class of one-pointed stable maps. Compute their generating functions through mirror periods, exchanging vertical flux on Y4 with horizontal flux on its mirror.

Late-time analysis separates homogeneous and inhomogeneous corrections to the squeezing angle. Their competition changes at β=1/2 for accelerating expansion and β=−1/2 for decelerating contraction, producing logarithmic corrections at the thresholds.

Nielsen's geometric method with geodesic weighting evaluates complexity from Gaussian reference and target widths, retaining inverse-tangent terms for complex frequencies. The reference frequencies are ω_k=ω_−k=k/2.

Solve hypercharge anomaly-cancellation conditions together with gauge invariance of Yukawa interactions. The conditions include mixed nonabelian–hypercharge anomalies, the cubic hypercharge anomaly, and the mixed gauge–gravitational anomaly, whose redundancy depends on the scenario.

Use the homogeneous-field Schwinger rate, integrate pair-production and acceleration power over the vacuum gap, add persistent luminosity, and require this expenditure not exceed electromagnetic reservoir energy divided by active lifetime. The approximate inequality is solved numerically.

Volterra iteration analyzes an initially conformal-like vacuum. For spectra, WKB data at a matching time define exact zeroth-, second-, or fourth-order adiabatic states; numerical evolution determines their late-time coefficients in an asymptotic Bunch–Davies basis.

Bogoliubov coefficients and adiabatic subtraction isolate the state-dependent energy density of a massive conformally coupled scalar. Appendix A splits its momentum integral into infrared and ultraviolet pieces and bounds their early-time differences.
Dimensional reduction supplies V(ρ,τ,σ1,σ2) and a non-diagonal positive field metric. At a critical point, eigenvalues of g⁻¹∂²V diagnose tachyons; the analysis freezes other scalar fluctuations.

The orientifold-restricted equations comprise 46 scalar equations in 43 variables, including flux equations, Bianchi identities, Einstein/dilaton equations, and Jacobi identities. Constrained minimization of squared residuals, followed by local refinement, searches for R4>0 and T10³≤0.
Lie-algebra identification uses nilradicals and changes of basis, followed by lattice-existence results to establish compact quotients for selected solutions.

Use seven-dimensional anomaly inflow to explain the difference between regularizations. Compare the quantum circle-reduction prepotential with the classical M-theory prepotential obtained from divisor triple intersections in an F-theory-adapted basis.

Integrate out massive Kaluza-Klein towers through parity-violating triangle amplitudes. Compare zeta regularization and mode-by-mode five-dimensional Pauli-Villars regulators with the circle reduction of a six-dimensional Pauli-Villars regulator.

Perform classical circle reduction, dualize the reduced two-forms into vectors using the inherited self-duality equations, and pass to five-dimensional Einstein frame. The classical Green-Schwarz terms produce non-gauge-invariant, scalar-dependent Chern-Simons couplings.

The solution phase space method uses kξ = δQξ − ξ·Θ and defines δS = T_BH^−1 ∫H kξH. Perturbations satisfy the linearized field equations; the temperature is supplied separately. Integrability over solution parameters and agreement with the first law provide the reported consistency tests.

A decomposition along constant-φ hypersurfaces separates intrinsic curvature and extrinsic-curvature terms. The authors use their coefficients as a shortcut to the direction-dependent graviton speeds, rather than presenting a full linearized perturbation analysis.

Choose a positive loitering sphere radius, solve the reduced equations from horizon-compatible initial data, and verify the Hamiltonian constraint. Express V(t) as V(χ) where trajectory inversion is consistent.
Eliminate cyclic-coordinate velocities using symmetry, impose the causal norm, and examine the proper-time or affine-parameter integral. Keep the null and timelike normalizations distinct.

The likelihood combines Planck 2018 temperature, polarization, and lensing data; BOSS DR12 consensus BAO at effective redshifts 0.38, 0.51, and 0.61; Pantheon supernovae; and a Gaussian SH0ES prior H0 = 74.03 ± 1.42 km s−1 Mpc−1. These are the historical inputs to the reported inference.

MontePython-v3 interfaced with a modified CLASS performs Metropolis–Hastings MCMC over six standard cosmological parameters plus fEDE, log10 zc, and Θi. Chains use the Gelman–Rubin criterion R − 1 < 0.01. Scalar perturbations are evolved exactly at linear order in synchronous gauge.

Estimate prefactors using translation zero modes and dimensional analysis rather than evaluating the full fluctuation determinants. The omitted center-of-mass spatial contribution is restored by hand.

Continue t→−iτ and apply the Callan–Coleman saddle-point method. The tunneling exponent is the bounce–false-vacuum Euclidean action difference; separated multiple bounces are summed in the dilute-gas approximation.

Find constant-H, constant-φ de Sitter solutions, then linearize the background equations in δH and δφ. Stability is diagnosed by negative real parts of both eigenvalues of the resulting 2×2 evolution matrix.

After imposing c_T=1, rescale h̃_e=a^λh_e and solve the approximate mode equation using Bessel/Hankel functions. An early-time Bunch–Davies condition selects the normalized positive-frequency solution.

Expand the action to quadratic order in transverse-traceless metric perturbations, Fourier transform, and examine the kinetic coefficient and dispersion relation. The displayed calculation orients the wavevector along z and uses the + and × polarizations.

Bounds couplings by requiring approximate gaplessness to survive mixing. Random-sign cancellations and Wigner-matrix scaling yield the within-sector estimate C̃≲ε₀/(√N_m√K); without random signs the energy-disturbance bound is stronger.

Uses the previously obtained analytic two-mode solution to quantify memory-burden suppression, then coupled 2×2 level-splitting estimates and iterative reasoning to explain why simultaneous master-mode depletion and memory transfer can remain inefficient.

Numerical evolution uses a Krylov-subspace method with a stated state-norm error bound of 10⁻⁶, relaxed to 10⁻⁵ for K=8. Parameter scans identify rewriting couplings and fit empirical rate scalings; these calculations are not reproduced here.

Sample field-history coefficients, reject uncontrolled expansions, fit the remaining histories and apply potential and observational cuts. Compare fitted H0 and χ² with ΛCDM, then repeat selected robustness variations.

Compute the density and potential histories for each nonphantom CPL pair, integrate the scalar trajectory and combine these parametric functions. The application fixes the density ratio to 3/7 and the present field origin to zero.

Choose scalar-history coefficients, substitute their series into the redshift background equations and solve order by order. The application constructs potential deformations near ΛCDM without imposing slow roll or choosing a fixed global potential shape.

Filter imported CPL chains, reconstruct each potential trajectory, and bin and spline its field-dependent summaries. This extends the reviewed reconstruction into a comparison of potentials selected by combined early- and late-time data.

Match a physical mass power to the canonical quadratic action, infer the kinetic metric, convert volume powers to field exponentials, and expand around a reference vacuum. The output applies only within the diagonal-sector, fixed-prefactor, leading-volume ansatz.

Represent tower existence through extra operator-density growth below the black-hole regime, then ask whether CFT consistency enforces that feature. The source supplies a qualitative LVS application and cited precedents, while leaving higher-dimensional necessity unresolved.

Compute cubic bulk Witten diagrams using embedding-space propagators to extract three-point OPE coefficients. Both derivative axion couplings and, where present, nonderivative φa² interactions enter the mixed coefficient.

Use Mellin amplitudes, conformal-block logarithms and Mack-polynomial projection to obtain tree-level n=0 anomalous dimensions. Large-spin asymptotics follow from exchange poles; the analytic-in-spin formula excludes contact-term contributions.

Differentiate the constrained cosine potential, solve common-sine stationarity and classify extrema with the reduced Hessian. Its rank-one structure makes determinant positivity sufficient after imposing the subordinate-phase sign conditions.

Integrate out massive fields coupled to a much lighter scalar, estimate induced local potential coefficients, and compare them with the coefficients required by the proposed infrared dynamics. Here the massive fields are pions and the required scalar mass is cosmological.

Vary the lightest-quark phase at fixed mass ratios, generate subordinate phases and retain positive-slope crossings of −θ modulo 2π. Compare their energies before identifying excited metastable states.

Generate discrete shifted branches from a large-parameter ansatz, then minimize over the labels to obtain the physical energy. In this application the labels represent Yang–Mills branches; the operation does not determine their finite-Nc tunnelling rates or local stability.

Remove longitudinal gauge directions, invert the transverse quadratic operator, and contract it with pullback source tensors. The paper first establishes the single-form normalization and then adapts the tensor calculation to mixed three-forms.

Differentiate the source tension at fixed charges, contract the resulting real-scalar vertices, and then use holomorphy to reorganize the answer. The explicit BPS calculation assumes K=K(Z+bar Z) and T=2e^(K/2)|W|.

Linearize the source coupling, gauge-fix and invert the mediator kinetic operator, then contract the two source insertions. The paper applies this reviewed operation separately to scalar, graviton and form exchange before summing the amplitudes.

A York constraint construction starts from a conformally flat spatial metric and freely specified conformally rescaled trace-free extrinsic-curvature data. The conformal factor and remaining shear data are obtained by solving the gravitational constraints.

Periodic initial data use 0≤x≤2π and Q(x,t0)=Θ[f1 cos(m1x+d1)+Q0]. Nonlinearity is measured by Δf=f1/Qattr and ΔQ=|Q0−Qattr|/Qattr, taken to be O(1); the homogeneous offset Q0 is the key change from the earlier study.

Numerical evolution of the full 3+1 Einstein–scalar equations uses Hubble-normalized variables and constant-mean-curvature hypersurfaces, tracking initial curvature, matter density and shear over up to several hundred Hubble-radius e-folds.

The holographic calculation solves linearized bulk-plus-brane propagation with Neumann boundary conditions, interior regularity and brane matching. Visible-sector quantum corrections induce a brane kinetic term; the resulting propagator resums bulk and brane contributions.

Expand the current-current coupling through O(λ²), use connected hidden-current correlators and their Källén–Lehmann representation, and Fourier-transform the static interaction. Free massive scalar and fermion examples employ Wick contractions, Feynman parameters and dimensional regularization.

Construct a background-gauge-invariant Schwinger functional, derive its Ward identities, and Legendre-transform the vector source to a current expectation value. A nonlinear coupled-sector construction is compared with the original induced action after extremizing the emergent vector.

The authors construct globally defined one-forms from Maurer–Cartan equations, identify allowed lattice gluings, count orientifold fixed points, and compute closed and co-closed forms with constant coefficients. Harmonic representatives and their cycle integrals provide the flux normalization.

A Hodge decomposition separates harmonic, exact, and coexact flux pieces. Numerical searches then translate fixed supergravity data into coupling, radii, a rescaling parameter, and quantized data, with selected constraints relaxed to identify conflicts. Scaling transformations illustrate parameter-space bounds rather than establish an exhaustive no-go theorem.

Coarse grain discrete production events using their event rate and memory kernel, then solve terminal force balance. Compute force and energy with their respective weights; reusing one expression for both changes the inferred inflationary constraints.

Use internal gauge directions to construct a background compatible with spatial isotropy and reduce the field equations. The literal source claim excluding homogeneous U(1) fields is too strong; a single homogeneous Abelian vector generally fails isotropy instead.

Determine two transition temperatures, verify their ordering, and translate their ratio into e-folds using the temperature-redshift law. This operation requires a specified bath evolution; it cannot be transferred unchanged to a continuously heated bath.
Compactify the string, map the state through F/M/IIA duality, and evaluate the wrapped heterotic formula. The paper substitutes this probe for a fourfold mirror-period calculation.
Translate wrapped objects and degeneration data using fiberwise M/heterotic duality and heterotic/F-theory duality, then use the frame with accessible cycle and anomaly information.
Excise generic K3 fibers from compatible blocks, identify the resulting cylindrical ends, exchange their circle factors, and match their K3 forms through the specified rotation.

Solve and normalize mirror periods, match their asymptotics, then analytically continue the appropriate charge combination. The paper describes this approach but uses a wrapped-string mass argument for its fourfold application.

The displayed extended-mass prescription is ∫ψ(M)/fmax(M) dM ≤ 1. It must be applied separately to each observable over its applicable mass interval; its preceding derivation and definitions are not fully supplied.

Gaussian horizon-scale fluctuations give β ≈ Erfc[δc/(√2 σ)]. The review contrasts the simple radiation-era estimate δc ≈ 1/3 with numerical/analytical estimates near 0.45; the threshold depends on perturbation profile, equation of state and non-Gaussianity.

Near-critical collapse uses M = K(δ − δc)^η, with K of order the horizon mass and η universal for a specified equation of state. The reviewed radiation case has δc ≈ 0.4 and η ≈ 0.35, producing a low-mass tail.

Reduce a product-metric curvature calculation by proving the mixed connection components vanish and performing contractions within each factor. The simplification requires independent coordinate dependence and cannot be transferred directly to warped or off-diagonal metrics.

Factor out a common coordinate scale, compute the logarithmic metric-velocity matrix, and use spacetime-constant invariants to simplify the averaged geodesic equation. The remaining off-diagonal equation must still be integrated correctly.

Choose a flow operator, compute the full curvature tensors, and reduce the tensor equation within a controlled metric ansatz. A scalar or single-component equation is sufficient only when the remaining components and coordinate dependence have also been checked.

Remove the horizon coordinate singularity by a tortoise integral, null coordinates and surface-gravity exponentiation. For flow calculations, distinguish fixed Kruskal coordinates from fixed areal radius because the transformation depends on evolving metric parameters.

Match the induced thermal boundary data of thermal AdS and Schwarzschild–AdS, regulate both radial integrals, subtract their actions, and compare the resulting free energies within the retained-saddle approximation.

Track roots of the implicit G-scaling equation at one fixed areal-radius sample, construct k=r_+/α, and count crossings of k=1. The source varies initial k and γ and reports an additional qualitative check under changes of the sample radius.

Illustrate the coupled product-radius equations at fixed dimensions and initial radii while varying γ over four selected values. The comparison includes ordinary Ricci flow and a large-negative-γ example intended to approach Yamabe-like behavior after suitable rescaling.
Use rank-weighted tensor-product connection formulas and known flat-bundle invariants on lens-space special Lagrangian cycles to construct fractional contributions for non-flat bundles.

Construct smooth, everywhere invertible patch matrices intertwining transition functions. Explicit isomorphisms between rank-two line-bundle sums on P1 are extended to ambient products and restricted to Calabi-Yau submanifolds.
Split connection changes into additive steps. Steps preserving F^(0,2) = 0 along the entire path contribute zero, leaving the genuinely non-holomorphic bundle identification to compute.
Modify CAMB only in its primordial-spectrum input and compare temperature autocorrelation spectra while retaining fixed late-time cosmological parameters.

Apply Airy-function uniform approximations to mode equations, including the complex frequency q² = k² − 2iλ_k. Expand Hubble flow functions about the turning point and then a common horizon-crossing pivot.

Use Gaussian Schrödinger wavefunctions for y = aδφ and compute ensemble-averaged squared means through 〈y〉² = 〈y²〉 − [4 Re(A_k)]^−1, with ensemble averaging understood. Moment equations and a Gaussian-width Riccati equation replace direct stochastic state evolution.

Shoot along alternating Euclidean and Lorentzian segments, tune the imaginary initial scalar, and iterate to reported residual precision 10⁻⁸. Estimate action derivatives by finite differences; choose a moderate endpoint size to balance reality conditions against accumulated numerical error.

Differentiate the complex saddle action with respect to boundary geometry and scalar data. Compare amplitude and phase gradients before assigning a classical history and an associated relative probability.

Tune complex initial scalar data, solve the Euclidean equations along a complex contour, and evaluate S_E. Reality at the endpoint supplies the boundary conditions; singularities and branch cuts restrict contour choices.

Approximate conditioning on an observed region by a spatial-volume factor, then compare the weighted densities of different histories. The paper separates classical slow-roll extrapolation from an assumption about stochastic eternal inflation.
Use an orthonormal one-form basis and imported Ricci components to extract radial pressure from the five-dimensional Einstein equations, setting factors 1−b/r to zero at r=r0.

Integrate the Einstein density equation using a noncommutative particle-source profile to obtain a shape function; then introduce a separately translated density profile to model the smeared throat surface.

Use constant-redshift f(R) field equations, a logarithmic f(R) expression imported from earlier work, a Maclaurin expansion, and an approximate power-law ansatz to argue for a large positive radial derivative of F=df/dR.

Convert an entropy constraint into a potential envelope using the actual cosmological evolution law. A logarithmic slope can be extracted when saturation or the derivative of the envelope gap is controlled; the source does not supply that extra condition.

Dress a non-conformal set of world-sheet couplings with a dynamical scale, impose one physical time, and translate the dressed equations into cosmology. Here the retained local fields are the graviton and dilaton.

Choose a microscopic conformal endpoint, match the leading dilaton exponential and its normalization, then seek a dressed world-sheet flow to it. The paper supplies asymptotic potential matching but does not construct a consistent interpolating solution.

Continue the supercritical background equations to a subcritical sign choice, return to real cosmic time, and choose a positive integration constant. The source does not specify full branch, boundary or reality conditions.

Chiral–linear multiplet duality and a Legendre transformation simplify coordinate-degenerate Kähler potentials with mixed axionic and other fields. In the linear formulation the relevant no-scale identity is L^I KI=3.

Homogeneity differentiation relates scaling to K^{i j̄}KiKj̄. Reviewing an earlier result, the authors use a zero eigenvalue of MAB̄=∂A∂B̄e^{−G/3} as the generalized no-scale criterion, with positive kinetic terms essential to the potential-sign argument.

Use crossing-symmetric forward scattering amplitudes around flat space with τ=i and vanishing gauge fields. Dispersion relations and the optical theorem constrain scalar, scalar-photon and four-photon coefficient combinations.

Evaluate the Euclidean action in the grand canonical ensemble on the uncorrected solution to obtain thermodynamics through first order in the Wilson coefficients. Transform to fixed charges and take T→0 to extract extremality corrections without solving the corrected field equations.

Quantum extremal surface prescription: S = min_X ext_X[Area(X)/(4G_N) + S_semi-cl(Σ_X)], with X codimension two and Σ_X bounded by X and the cutoff. Extremize in spacetime, then select the smallest extremal value. The review also describes a maximin construction over Cauchy slices.

Construct polynomial functions, apply their sign-kernel transforms, and combine them in a finite antisymmetrized sum. Construct graphical distributions of paired critical-point features, retain flux-case labels, and inspect their qualitative association. Figure 7 supplies the potential–coupling application; the potential–mass application begins on this page but has no supplied conclusion.

Evaluate all training cases, differentiate squared error through the sigmoid, and update against the gradient. The example uses learning rate one and every available Boolean input, so its error measures training reproduction rather than held-out prediction.
Optimize weights and biases on a random 80% training subset, reserving 10% for validation and 10% for testing. The objective is referenced to an unavailable appendix equation.

Plot the obtained critical points with population colors, enlarge the near-origin region, and compare occupied regions and line structures. The source reports qualitative inspection without a specified regression, clustering algorithm, distance metric, or statistical hypothesis test.

Linearize network residuals, choose damping by a trust-region procedure, solve for a regularized step, and iterate toward a local minimum. The displayed update requires clarification before implementing the displayed objective.

Compare a physically generated spectrum with a statistical matrix ensemble, then transfer stability probabilities only if the ensemble correspondence is justified. Here the proposed correspondence concerns flux-potential Hessians.

Use precomputed examples to train a candidate filter, screen a larger configuration collection, and directly solve only selected candidates. Here the filter learns flux patterns and the GA evaluates potential extrema and Hessians.

Use an ANN together with a genetic algorithm to locate flux configurations producing critical points, then classify energies and masses. The summary identifies the combined strategy without its full training, genetic-selection, acceptance, or verification sequence.

Use modular transformation to obtain vacuum-dominated high-temperature asymptotics, then an inverse Laplace transform and saddle-point evaluation for charged degeneracies. Determine the exact two-dimensional R-symmetry by c-extremizing the trial anomaly-derived central charge.

Construct horizons through symplectic quartic-invariant attractor equations and BPS Higgsing constraints that decouple a massive vector multiplet. The appendix also extremizes entropy functions assembled from gravitational blocks; the authors report agreement with their explicit horizon solutions.

Apply the Iyer-Wald Noether-charge variational identity in the Sorce-Wald infall setup. Integrating over the horizon segment and late-time hypersurface expresses δM−ΦHδQ as a horizon matter-stress flux, which is nonnegative under the matter NEC.

Compare the tangent inequality preventing motion past the corrected extremality curve with the minimum energy-to-charge requirement for matter crossing the horizon. A minimally coupled test particle provides the initial illustration.

Taylor-expand λ around v in ln(φ/v). Retain the linear logarithm for β(v)>0, λ(v)<0, or the squared logarithm when β(v)=λ(v)=0. These define the first- and second-order CW models.
Combine first-order slow-roll observables with numerical endpoint and e-fold calculations. Scan both φ>v and φ<v branches, imposing A_s≈2.1×10⁻⁹ throughout the reported numerical results.
